title: Whom Do AI Agents Work For? Role Assignment Induces Sponsorship Bias in LLM Recommenders
abstract: arXiv:2609.17989v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now serve as conversational shopping assistants on platforms that also sell advertising. These AI agents face a conflict of duty. They advise consumers who rely on their judgment, yet are deployed by platforms that benefit when sponsored listings are chosen. Sponsorship disclosures, designed to allow consumers to penalize paid placements, now reach the AI agent rather than the consumer, and the agent's evaluation of them is hidden from the consumer. Drawing on the fiduciary concept of conflict of duty, we argue that an agent's evaluation of a sponsored listing should not depend on which party deployed it. In controlled choice experiments, we manipulate assigned roles in the system prompt to name either a traveler or a booking platform as the agent's principal. Platform delegation significantly attenuates the penalty that agents apply to sponsored listings and weakens the skepticism that disclosure triggers

translated_title: AI智能体为谁服务？角色分配在LLM推荐系统中引发赞助偏见
translated_abstract: 大型语言模型（LLM）如今在同时销售广告的平台充当对话式购物助手。这些AI智能体面临职责冲突：它们为依赖其判断的消费者提供建议，却由在赞助商品被选中时获益的平台所部署。旨在让消费者能够惩罚付费广告位的赞助披露信息，如今传达给了AI智能体而非消费者，而智能体对这些披露的评估过程对消费者是隐蔽的。借鉴受托责任中的职责冲突概念，我们认为智能体对赞助商品的评价不应取决于部署它的是哪一方。在受控选择实验中，我们通过操纵系统提示中分配的角色，将旅行者或预订平台指定为智能体的委托人。结果显示，平台委托显著削弱了智能体对赞助商品施加的惩罚，并弱化了披露信息本应引发的怀疑态度。
tldr: 该研究发现，当LLM推荐系统被告知其委托人是平台而非消费者时，会显著降低对赞助商品的惩罚力度并弱化怀疑态度，表明AI智能体的角色分配会诱发赞助偏见，从而损害消费者利益。
en_tdlr: This study finds that when LLM recommenders are told their principal is a platform rather than a consumer, they significantly attenuate the penalty applied to sponsored listings and weaken skepticism triggered by disclosures, demonstrating that role assignment induces sponsorship bias in AI agents.
